facts.claim: "68 (Live)" is on the compilation "Live at Bo Bash 2021" and runs 3:28. Spotify lists the release date as September 15, 2021 and the copyright as © 2021 Various Artists.
Deezer credits Nolan Taylor as the sole writer of "68 (Live)".
The live recording came out in 2021. Nolan Taylor released an official studio version of "68" on April 21, 2023, together with a "68 (Behind the Song)" video.
In the "Behind the Song" video, Taylor describes the painful relationship with his mother that inspired "68".
A live video of "68" went viral and caught the attention of Atlantic Records. The song addresses his relationship with his mother and the topic of addiction.
A 2023 live performance of "68" filmed in the backwoods of West Virginia for the radiowv channel has more than 4.8M views.
Taylor is from Blanchester, Ohio. He was raised by his father and older brother, and his mother struggled with mental health issues and addiction.
Taylor picked up his first guitar, a left-handed one, in high school. He grew up on bluegrass and country, and on rock acts such as the Grateful Dead, Pinegrove, Alice in Chains and Nirvana.

Taylor made his full-length debut with the self-titled album Nolan Taylor in January 2025. His 2023 EPs include Life & Love, and Atlantic also issued the Live From The Living Room EP, which has a new version of "68".
The Herald-Dispatch places Taylor in the vein of Tyler Childers, Sturgill Simpson, Zach Bryan and Chris Stapleton. It also says he was signed to Atlantic Records and had played the Grand Ole Opry.

research.lineage: It sits in the raw, autobiographical alt-country, folk and Americana songwriting tradition of Tyler Childers, Sturgill Simpson and Zach Bryan.

draft:
A kid in the seventh grade is behind the wheel because his mother is nodding off driving down 68, and he takes over "just to get us back safe." That is the first scene of **68 (Live)**, and Nolan Taylor sets it down plainly. The verse opens by crediting her with his first cigarettes, then puts the child in the driver's seat as she falls asleep. The song never calls this neglect. It doesn't have to.

Taylor wrote it alone. He grew up in Blanchester, Ohio, raised by his father and older brother while his mother struggled with mental health and addiction, and he has said the song comes out of that painful relationship. The second verse is built from small, exact details of a house running on empty. A school bus he doesn't want to ride home. Three days without much to eat. And one line that does the work of a whole paragraph: "Oven was heating the house if our electric was on." The "if" carries it. The kid isn't complaining. He is reporting how things worked.

Then the chorus turns, and the voice of the song shifts from that child to the adult he became. "I'm tired of being nice" admits something before it threatens anything: he has been nice for a long time, probably longer than he should have been. The sharpest line is "Love me when you need a high," a whole history of being wanted for the wrong reasons, followed by "I'm done spending my money on you." The grief and the anger sit right next to each other and never settle.

The third verse gives the song its saddest kind of joy. When his father was off work, they'd drive around "listening to tunes," happy because she couldn't find them. The car that nearly killed him in the first verse becomes the getaway. "My whole life I've been running from you" ties the two together.

Musically, the setting stays simple. A steady, picked acoustic strum carries it at a slow, unhurried pace. Taylor sings in a clear, mid-range voice with no harmonies and nothing dressed up. The delivery is conversational, closer to someone telling you about it than to a performance. The room is raw and you can hear it, which suits a song this unguarded. It belongs to the confessional alt-country of Tyler Childers, Sturgill Simpson and Zach Bryan, where the plainest line usually lands hardest. This live take predates his 2023 studio version by two years, and it already sounds finished.

Look at how the lyric ends. "I'm through with you" comes back over and over, as if saying it once isn't enough to make it true.

The song puts you in the passenger seat beside a child who had to be the adult, and then makes you watch that child, grown up, still trying to say goodbye.
